entry.title: X-rays: Connecting Invisible Dots to Unlock Discovery Paula Marie Ivey - Berkeley Lab Research SLAM

media:group.media:title: X-rays: Connecting Invisible Dots to Unlock Discovery Paula Marie Ivey - Berkeley Lab Research SLAM
media:group.media:description:
The 2026 Berkeley Lab Research SLAM was held on Wednesday, September 23, from 3:00–4:30 p.m. in Berkeley Lab’s Building 50 Auditorium.
SLAM alumni Syed Saqline and Thasneem Frousnoon co-hosted the culminating live event, where 12 early-career scientists delivered compelling three-minute talks about their research.
A distinguished panel of judges from academia, government, and industry selected the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd-place winners, while the in-person audience voted for the People’s Choice Award.
First place was awarded to Hakyung Lee of the Biosciences Area. Second place went to Adway Gupta of the Energy Science Area. Paula-Marie Ivey of the Energy Sciences Area won third place, and Mythili Surendran of the Energy Science Area won the People's Choice Award.More Berkeley Lab news: http://newscenter.lbl.gov Subscribe: https://youtube.com/berkeleylab

media:group.media:title: Behind the Science: RSoXS Beamline
media:group.media:description:
As the devices in our pockets and on our desks are expected to do more every year, the microchips inside them need to be more advanced, too. Researchers like Thomas Ferron and Qi Zhang are using beamline 11.0.1.2 at the Advanced Light Source, where resonant soft X-ray scattering can reveal buried nanostructures in polymers and other organic materials used in extreme UV photolithography. With this information, we provide the crucial ingredients to develop the microchips of the future. @berkeleylab #synchrotron #microchip #microelectronics #CenterForXRayOpticsMore

entry.title: Inside Berkeley Lab’s Advanced Light Source Upgrade

media:group.media:title: Inside Berkeley Lab’s Advanced Light Source Upgrade
media:group.media:description:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s (Berkeley Lab) Advanced Light Source produces bright beams of light used to study materials and molecules down to the atomic level. A state-of-the-art upgrade now underway will make that light not only brighter, but coherent: a property invisible to the naked eye, yet powerful enough to reveal atomic-scale anomalies in batteries, quantum materials, and more. This new precision aims to accelerate discovery across science disciplines.
This video explains how the ALS upgrade — with soft x-ray light that is 100x brighter and nearly fully coherent — will reveal a new level of scientific detail.
Credit: Cindy Lee and Jenny Weger/Berkeley Lab

media:group.media:title: Reverse Science Fair - Introduction
media:group.media:description:
In collaboration with Berkeley Lab's Early Career Employee Resource Group and Community Resources for Science, the Berkeley Lab A-Lift office flipped the traditional science fair. STEM and STEM adjacent professionals visit middle schools in the Bay Area and present their 'science project' for 8th-grade students to view and judge. Professionals have the opportunity to practice their communication skills, and students receive accessible introductions to STEM research and careers.

entry.title: SYNAPS-I Connects to the American Science Cloud

media:group.media:title: SYNAPS-I Connects to the American Science Cloud
media:group.media:description:
As part of the Department of Energy's (DOE) Genesis Mission, SYnergistic Neutron and Photon Science – Intelligence (SYNAPS-I) uses AI tools and state-of-the-art research techniques to accelerate discovery across national scientific user facilities.
By enabling real-time data interpretation during acquisition, the collaborative project is transforming how scientists use these facilities and how quickly they can publish results that benefit agriculture security, energy technologies, microelectronics, and more.
The collaborative effort is led by Berkeley Lab. The project includes scientists and users from Berkeley Lab, Argonne National Laboratory (ANL), Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), Stanford Linear Accelerator Center (SLAC), and Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL). entry.title: What’s the Problem with Quantum Noise? The Limit Holding #Quantum Computers Back

media:group.media:title: What’s the Problem with Quantum Noise? The Limit Holding #Quantum Computers Back
media:group.media:description:
What Is Quantum Noise? The Limit Holding Quantum Computers Back
Even in a perfectly isolated system, the universe still fluctuates. These tiny, unavoidable disturbances, known as quantum noise, set the ultimate limit on what we can measure and control at the smallest scales.
Learn what quantum noise is and how researchers are developing new techniques to understand and mitigate quantum noise, from novel qubit designs that stay stable longer to AI-powered measurement methods that improve how quantum systems are controlled.
The goal? Quantum computers powerful enough to discover new medicines and materials, and detectors sensitive enough to observe dark matter and neutrinos.
